articles.title: Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
articles.summary: Reduced missile warnings increase threat to civilians as Trump pushes an ‘energy ceasefire’ and peace negotiations.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.

This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.

The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.

But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.

He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.

The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.

The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.

“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).

Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.

“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.

The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.

Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.

On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.

Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.

“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.

Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.

Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries

The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.

It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.

However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.

“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.

However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.

No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.

“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.

However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.

Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.

Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.

Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.

On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.

Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).

The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.

Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.

Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.

“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”

In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.

In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.

Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

articles.title: America’s China lesson is reshaping its India policy
articles.summary: Much of India’s strategic establishment still sees Trump merely as an aberration, but this shift began under former President Joe Biden.
articles.body:
Washington does not want to make the same mistake twice.

Having helped China become an economic and technological powerhouse, only to create its greatest strategic rival, Washington now appears determined to approach India’s rise differently.

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau made the point during his New Delhi visit earlier this year. Landau stated bluntly that America would not make its China mistake again by allowing India to “develop all these markets” and capabilities, only to discover that India was “beating us in a lot of commercial things.”

The remarks echoed a broader reassessment in Washington of India’s rise. Two months earlier, the State Department’s five-year strategic plan made only one reference to India and declared that Washington would “seek partnership with growing regional economies such as India but on terms that advance U.S. security and economic interests and avoid repeating past mistakes.”

For two decades, Washington saw a rising democratic India as inherently good for the free world, especially as a counterweight to an increasingly autocratic and expansionist China. A stronger India also meant a larger market for American companies and a more capable Indo-Pacific partner. India was thus given pride of place in America’s Indo-Pacific strategy , first unveiled in 2017 .

Now, the administration no longer appears to view India’s rise as entirely benign. India’s role in U.S. policy is being downgraded, especially as President Trump adopts a more conciliatory approach to China , including recognizing it as America’s principal strategic peer.

The White House’s latest National Security Strategy , unlike previous iterations, demotes India’s role by making only a passing reference to the country. The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy , for its part, does not mention India at all, although New Delhi holds more annual military exercises with America than any other country. In another signal of India’s strategic downgrading, the Pentagon in June dropped the prefix “Indo” from “Indo-Pacific.”

India’s eroding salience in U.S. policy is also weakening the Quad, America’s strategic coalition with India, Japan and Australia. Increasingly marginal to U.S. strategy, the Quad risks strategic irrelevance . No Quad leaders’ summit has been held since 2024. Trump’s trade war against India derailed last year’s summit, and none has been scheduled this year. Trump’s own National Security Strategy reflects the Quad’s diminished standing, giving the grouping a single passing mention and only in relation to India.

Much of India’s strategic establishment still sees Trump merely as an aberration. They view his tariffs, pressure tactics and transactional approach to New Delhi as the excesses of an unusually disruptive president. Once Trump leaves office, the thinking goes, the U.S. and India can return to the trajectory that preceded him.

But that assumption mistakes a structural shift for a presidential interlude. The deeper shift in Washington’s thinking about India began in the latter half of Joe Biden’s presidency and is likely to outlast Trump.

As India’s power grew, disagreements over trade, U.S. policies in South Asia and New Delhi’s Ukraine-war neutrality spurred tensions . Trump has accelerated that shift and stripped away much of the diplomatic cushioning that once softened bilateral differences.

India, however, is no longer a relatively weak power whose strategic policies Washington can shape. India’s economy has almost quadrupled in real terms since 2000. India has also developed its own industrial ambitions, energy strategy, technology policies and geopolitical relationships. As a rising power, India seeks to preserve the freedom to make its own strategic choices.

Strategic autonomy is not uniquely Indian. Every major power safeguards its freedom of action, and America is no exception.

The problem, then, is not strategic autonomy itself. It is the growing tension between Washington’s expectation that India’s rise should reinforce American strategic objectives and New Delhi’s determination to ensure that its growing power expands rather than narrows its freedom of action.

Bilateral trade negotiations are currently deadlocked. India wants to become a manufacturing powerhouse, reduce external dependence and protect strategic industries. The U.S., on the other side, wants greater access to India’s enormous domestic market, the world’s largest and fastest-growing.

The tensions, however, are manageable, provided Washington does not mistake partnership for alignment and New Delhi does not confuse strategic autonomy with strategic defiance.

Washington’s experience with Beijing helps explain the renewed China analogy: It has changed how U.S. policymakers view economic interdependence. The old assumption was that helping a rising power become wealthier and more integrated into the global economy would make it a more responsible stakeholder and perhaps even a strategic partner.

The lesson Washington is drawing today is not necessarily that India’s rise should be stopped, but that America should be more careful about the terms on which it helps another major power rise. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to visit India early next week for the second time in five months.

The irony is that China is also taking steps to constrain India’s rise. This year, Beijing has imposed India-specific export curbs , widely seen as efforts to slow India’s emergence as an alternative global manufacturing hub. Leveraging its dominance of global supply chains , China has restricted exports to India of manufacturing equipment, industrial components, lithium-ion and battery technologies, and critical minerals.

India and the U.S. still need each other, but the relationship must be built on a more realistic foundation. For New Delhi, the test is to manage U.S. expectations without sacrificing its own interests. For Washington, it is to accept that a genuinely powerful India will sometimes make choices America dislikes.

Washington should recognize that a powerful India can be a valuable partner precisely because it is capable of acting independently. With the Trump administration asking U.S. allies to take greater responsibility for their own security , Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby declared , “India is a model ally that takes its own defense with utmost seriousness.”

America’s China lesson could ultimately strengthen the U.S.-India relationship. But that will happen only if Washington learns to distinguish an independent partner from a prospective rival, and New Delhi shows that autonomy need not preclude collaboration.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “Water: Asia’s New Battleground. “

articles.title: Lost piece of Jesus' world emerges after 2,000 years in extraordinary discovery
articles.summary: The Israel Antiquities Authority uncovered a 2,000-year-old aqueduct near Jerusalem that a biblical scholar believes has links to Jesus and early Christians.
articles.body: A 2,000-year-old aqueduct was recently uncovered near Jerusalem — and it likely supplied water used by Jesus and his disciples, according to a biblical scholar. Archaeologists unearthed a roughly 984-foot section of the ancient waterway south of Kibbutz Ramat Rachel — which once carried water from Solomon's Pools near Bethlehem to Jerusalem's Temple Mount. The discovery was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) on Oct. 11, following excavations ahead of a planned residential development. MASSIVE 2,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY FROM TIME OF JESUS EMERGES REMARKABLY INTACT Originally constructed during the Hasmonean period, the aqueduct remained in intermittent use until about a century ago, the IAA said. The waterway relied on gravity to transport water to the Second Temple complex, the center of Jewish religious life at the time, where it was used for ritual purification and cleaning up after sacrifices. The Second Temple complex was also the setting of the biblical account of Jesus cleansing the Temple, during which he overturned the tables of money changers and drove out merchants. The Lower Aqueduct was "probably built in the time of the Hasmonean kings to supply water to Jerusalem," according to excavation directors Benyamin Storchan, Gil Freid and Rotem Cohen of the Israel Antiquities Authority. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 'MYSTERIOUS' ANCIENT TUNNEL NEAR BIBLICAL KINGDOM OF JUDAH SITE IN JERUSALEM "The aqueduct runs about 21 km [13 miles] from Solomon's Pools, south of Bethlehem, to Jerusalem," the directors said in a statement. "Along most of the route, the water flowed along a very gentle gradient, dropping just one meter [3.3 feet] in elevation per kilometer [0.6 miles]." The aqueduct will be preserved and incorporated into the main entrance of the planned residential development, allowing visitors to see the ancient engineering firsthand. articles.summary: Ukraine resumed drone attacks on Russian refineries Thursday after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump was over. articles.body:
Ukraine resumed drone attacks on Russian refineries Thursday after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump was over.

The attack struck a refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov posted on Telegram, according to Reuters .

“The material damage is now being assessed,” Malkov wrote online. “Emergency services are working ​at the scene.”

A senior Ukrainian official confirmed the attack to The Associated Press .

Zelensky, who has expressed his frustration over the deal reached between the U.S. and Russia to allow diesel to enter the U.S. and global marketplace amid a worldwide energy shortage, told Financial Times Thursday that Ukraine’s patience had run out.

“The block is out. We’re done,” he told the outlet.

Zelensky also told British journalist Piers Morgan on his YouTube series “ Uncensored ” on Wednesday that he felt betrayed by Trump’s diesel deal with Putin and with the slowdown to restore satellite speeds via SpaceX’s Starlink services.

“Really, yes, between us,” Zelensky said, when Morgan asked if he felt betrayed. “Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump. … Energy ceasefire, it’s OK, it’s understandable.”

He added, “It’s the worst version of peace but, anyway, it’s some steps to the peace.”

The Ukrainian leader called the Trump administration’s behavior “really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us.”

Ukraine’s former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Wednesday that SpaceX was restoring speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour in a social media post .

Zelensky added later in the “Uncensored” interview that the slowdown was a “big mistake” and warned that Ukrainians could die if speeds were not restored.

The Ukrainian leader also told Morgan that the U.S. is not “on the right side of history.”

“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side but we are OK that he’s in the middle,” he continued. “But if you’re in the middle you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side. I think his advisers are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side. This is not right side of history.”

Zelensky blasted Trump’s deal last Friday as a “gift” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying that Russia “will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”

But Trump also faced opposition to the deal from Republican lawmakers who said they received no consultation or warning from the administration about the deal. They pointed to a 2022 statute banning Russian energy imports.

“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), John Curtis (Utah), Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Alan Armstrong (Okla.) and Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden (Ore.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.) said in a joint statement .

Tillis on Wednesday also pressed the Pentagon’s inspector general to look into the Starlink issues and asked Musk for more transparency on the issue.

articles.title: Photos: China and North Korea open new border bridge amid deepening ties
articles.summary: The New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong, China, and Sinuiju, North Korea, enhancing regional trade and collaboration.
articles.body:
The opening of a long-delayed bridge linking China and North Korea underscores the deepening ties between the two neighbours as Pyongyang courts both Beijing and Moscow to ease its economic isolation.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said a launch ceremony was held on Thursday for the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju.

Video from state media showed trucks decorated with the national flags of both countries lined up on the four-lane span, which itself was festooned with Chinese and North Korean flags.

In a video address, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed the bridge as a “new landmark” of the countries’ “traditional friendship” and urged both sides to use the opening to deepen connectivity and explore new cooperation in border areas, Xinhua reported. North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also delivered a video message.

The 3km (1.8-mile) road bridge is expected to ease pressure on the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a decades-old structure on the same route that carries a railway line and vehicles but can accommodate only one-way traffic at a time.

More than 70 percent of official trade between the two countries currently goes through that crossing, according to Chinese data. The South Korean government has counted at least 17 active road and rail links along the 1,400km (870-mile) North Korea-China border.

images.caption: A Chinese patrol vessel travels along the Yalu River as trucks adorned with Chinese flags cross the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge into North Korea's Sinuiju from China's Dandong New Zone, as seen from Dandong, Liaoning province, China. [Florence Lo/Reuters]

The New Yalu River Bridge was completed on the Chinese side about 2014 and initially was expected to open that year. But no corresponding work was carried out in Sinuiju, and the project stalled for more than a decade. [Florence Lo/Reuters]
A truck adorned with North Korean flags enters the Chinese side of the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge. [Florence Lo/Reuters]
Dandong residents come to see the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge. [Florence Lo/Reuters]

The delay in the bridge's opening fuelled speculation that Pyongyang was wary of increased economic dependence on China or displeased that Beijing backed United Nations sanctions resolutions targeting North Korea’s nuclear and missile programmes. Some analysts also suggested the two governments had disagreed over the location of the crossing. [Florence Lo/Reuters]

Frustration over the holdup was notable even in Chinese state-linked media. The Communist Party-affiliated Global Times carried unusually sharp comments from Dandong residents who had hoped the bridge would bring an economic boost to the border city. [Florence Lo/Reuters]

articles.title: Albania rioters clash with police for Socialist government as European unrest spreads
articles.summary: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama vowed not to resign as protests in Tirana erupted for a third day, with police deploying tear gas and water cannons.
articles.body: Clashes between police and protesters who are against Albania's Socialist government erupted in the country's capital for the third consecutive day Thursday as Prime Minister Edi Rama vowed he will not resign. Rioters in Tirana were seen throwing rocks at a police cordon outside Albania's Education Ministry, prompting law enforcement to respond with tear gas and water cannons, according to The Associated Press. The clashes followed riots on Wednesday when protesters attacked government buildings, banks and businesses, leaving 89 people injured, including 61 police officers. "As for calls for my resignation, governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution," Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama told Reuters on Thursday. ALBANIAN PROTESTERS FLOOD STREETS DEMANDING PRIME MINISTER'S RESIGNATION AMID CORRUPTION ACCUSATIONS "My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward," he added. "The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership." Thursday's protests included student groups seeking education reforms, as well as others staging a broader anti-government movement opposed to a major development project linked to President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, the AP reported. The so-called flamingo movement is calling for the resignation of Rama over allegations of widespread corruption. The movement earned the name after protesters used signs depicting the pink bird. "The message from the streets is clear: Albanians have had enough. Public patience with Edi Rama’s socialist government has come to an end," Agim Nesho, former Albanian ambassador to the United States, told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "The wheels are coming off Edi Rama’s socialist government. After 13 years in power, his administration faces mounting accusations of corruption, misuse of public funds, and political favoritism," Nesho said. "Meanwhile, poverty, unemployment, inadequate public services, and the mass exodus of young Albanians seeking better opportunities in Europe have fueled widespread anger. Critics argue that, as with other failed socialist governments, the political elite has benefited while ordinary citizens have been left struggling to make ends meet." An EU delegation in Albania called late Wednesday for a proportionate response from authorities, expressing concern at "the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana." JARED KUSHNER'S OVERSEAS LUXURY RESORT PROJECT FACES ANTI-CORRUPTION INVESTIGATION DURING VIOLENT PROTESTS Rama won his fourth term as prime minister last year, running on a platform centered around Albania joining the EU, which it hopes to achieve as early as 2028, according to Reuters. Student organizers told Reuters that the protests are over higher education costs, a lack of financial support, conditions at universities and job prospects after graduating. The prime minister said to the news agency that he is ready to discuss the cost of education, but added, "Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students." "Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania's European future." articles.title: Police shooting, water shortages, rising costs: Mauritius extends curfew amid unrest
articles.summary: Mauritius on Thursday extended a curfew for a further two nights following unrest triggered by the police shooting of a woman, as the African island
articles.body: Mauritius on Thursday extended a curfew for a further two nights following unrest triggered by the police shooting of a woman, as the African island nation grapples with protests over water shortages and the rising cost of living.The demonstrations began last week and escalated after a police officer shot and wounded a 27-year-old woman in Camp Levieux, a densely populated residential neighbourhood about 15 kilometres (9 miles) south of the capital, Port Louis.The officer was arrested and taken into custody as authorities launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the shooting. However, the incident fuelled further tensions, prompting authorities to impose an initial curfew from 8:30 pm on Tuesday until 6 am on Wednesday.Police are set to strengthen their presence, particularly in areas affected by violence, while reinforcing roadblocks and vehicle checkpoints, according to a government statement.“Police will step up measures and will act firmly, as appropriate, to contain further escalation of violence,” the statement said.Over 100 arrested in 2 days; schools shutThe Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam, cited a police report indicating that 94 people had been arrested through Tuesday, including 16 minors and one police officer. Police reported 26 additional arrests during Wednesday night’s operations and confirmed that all roads were clear of obstructions by Thursday morning.The Cabinet also warned that those arrested could face charges under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, where applicable. Authorities have also established a process to expedite cases following consultations with judicial and law enforcement officials.Police were monitoring social media for hate speech and incitement to violence. Citing the involvement of minors in the unrest, the Cabinet indicated that it would consider amending the Children’s Act to lower the minimum age for detention and prosecution from 14 to 12.The education ministry announced the cancellation of school classes across Mauritius on Thursday and Friday due to security concerns. Some primary and secondary school examinations scheduled for those days were also postponed in Mauritius and the neighbouring islands of Rodrigues and Agaléga, while international examinations would proceed as planned.Tourism and financial services under pressureTourism and financial services are key pillars of Mauritius’ economy. The island nation, regarded as one of Africa’s most stable democracies, experienced similar unrest in 1999, when the death of a popular musician in police custody triggered several days of rioting.Britain and Canada advised travellers to steer clear of demonstrations, warning of potential transport disruptions. Canada cautioned that further protests could erupt with “little or no warning.” The US Embassy in Port Louis issued a security alert on Tuesday, announcing the cancellation of scheduled services and advising visitors to arrange appointments in advance.Anger mounts over water shortages and rising costsThe unrest reflects growing public frustration over water shortages and the rising cost of living. On October 8, the government reported that reservoir levels had fallen to 57.1% of capacity, compared with 87.4% a year earlier. Mare aux Vacoas, one of the country’s key reservoirs, stood at just 35.7% capacity. Emergency measures announced by authorities include drilling boreholes and deploying water tankers.Statistics Mauritius reported that annual inflation climbed to 4.1% in September, up from 3.4% a year earlier, partly driven by higher petrol and food prices.The government also imposed restrictions on fuel sales in portable containers, while allowing motorists to refuel their vehicles as usual.You use AI every day. articles.title: What Chinese viewers are learning from America’s political chaos
articles.summary: What many Chinese viewers see is not a nation falling apart, but a freedom they have never been allowed to have at home.
articles.body:
Chinese viewers see America’s political chaos differently from Westerners: as a civics lesson forbidden at home.

I know the feeling. When I left China as a 26-year-old graduate student, my faith in the Communist Party shattered the moment my first plane, a Boeing 747, lifted into the sky; a display of industrial power China could not match. For viewers raised in a closed, leader-centered society, the American show is full of surprises that Westerners take for granted.

Even behind the Great Firewall, American politics has never been more visible in China. Clips of White House briefings, court rulings and congressional hearings circulate on Weibo and WeChat, often with Chinese subtitles, until the censors catch up; others climb over the wall with VPNs.

Political chaos is routine in democracies, but the Trump administration has made it especially dramatic, with a running series of clashes between the president, Congress and the courts. In February, the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency powers law he invoked did not authorize his sweeping tariffs; in June, it struck down his order restricting birthright citizenship. No side wins every round, and no one can cancel the series.

Many Americans are tired of the fighting, but people in China are watching and quietly drawing lessons. Five stand out.

First, everyday life goes on despite political turmoil. In China, where the party controls the government, schools, businesses and nearly every other institution, upheaval at the top shakes every corner of daily life, as the Cultural Revolution showed. American life largely goes on, and the country keeps leading the world in innovation.

Second, something stands above the ruler. Chinese tradition is human-centered and secular: Heaven and the ancestors were invoked, but no authority stood above the emperor. America’s founders declared that people are “endowed by their Creator” with rights that no government grants and none may take away. Whether one grounds these rights in God or in natural law, the effect is the same: The ruler is not the highest authority. When American politicians invoke these principles, Chinese viewers hear something new, and often inspiring.

Third, facts make the decision in court. In Chinese tradition, authorities define words and concepts, and facts are made to fit. American courts decide cases on evidence and law, argued in the open by opposing sides. A judge asks what happened and what the statute says, not which outcome serves the correct ideology. In China, verdicts follow the party line, and conviction rates exceed 99 percent .

Fourth, there is the rule of law, not of men. In China, law is an instrument the party uses to govern the people, never to bind those who govern. In America, the president himself can be sued, and he is legally bound to comply when he loses. These checks bind presidents of both parties: In 2023, the Supreme Court struck down Joe Biden’s student loan forgiveness plan, just as it has blocked Donald Trump’s tariffs. Despite repeated attempts to bend the rules, the separation of powers still works much as the founders designed.

Finally, there’s the freedom to speak and to organize. China’s constitution grants these rights on paper only. Every newspaper answers to the party, independent groups are suppressed and protests such as the 2022 “white paper” demonstrations against zero-COVID rules are quickly crushed. American newspapers criticize the president daily, comedians mock him nightly and citizens organize, protest and sue the government without asking permission.

Beijing’s state media present all this as proof that democracy breeds chaos and that “the East is rising and the West is declining.” On Chinese social media, only voices supporting the official line survive. Dissent is silenced: the Nobel Peace Prize laureate Liu Xiaobo died in state custody in 2017, and the outspoken property tycoon Ren Zhiqiang is serving an 18-year sentence .

Even China’s artificial intelligence is censored. When I asked the chatbot DeepSeek about Liu, it returned nothing. I asked about Ren, and it left out the essay widely seen as the real reason for his imprisonment, in which he was understood to call Xi Jinping “a clown stripped naked who insisted on continuing being emperor.”

No one can measure what people inside China truly think, because dissent carries a heavy price, and many Chinese abroad stay cautious too. But those who dare to speak freely tell a different story. The American chaos is real, yet it is the visible surface of something harder to see: liberty, power checking power and a society free enough to keep inventing. The noise is the sound of a nation arguing with itself rather than obeying one man or one party.

What many Chinese viewers see is not a nation falling apart, but a freedom they have never been allowed to have at home.

Yan Zhou, who grew up in China and earned a Ph.D. in mathematical economics from UCLA under Nobel laureate Lloyd S. Shapley, is an independent researcher in Seattle and the author of “From Scripts to Worldviews.”

articles.title: Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy mistrial says he has felt harassed
articles.summary: Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s high-profile murder trial, said he has been harassed since the trial ended in September.
articles.body: The lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s high-profile murder trial said he had been harassed since the trial ended in September, and doubled down on his stance that he did not have reasonable doubt during deliberations. The juror, Michael P. Desronvil, was the sole holdout who wanted to convict Clancy in the strangulation deaths of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — in January 2023, other jurors have said since the judge declared a mistrial in the case last month. “It was like night and day,” Desronvil said of his life before and after becoming the holdout juror. He spoke with Kayleigh McEnany on “Fox & Friends” on Thursday — his first media appearance since serving on the jury. Other jurors have described a man they claimed was unwilling to negotiate and hostile in the deliberation room. They said that Desronvil was insistent on convicting Clancy of the murders, but that he was not following the standard of reasonable doubt and had been blocking a unanimous decision. Through his attorney, Edward Andrew Paltzik, Desronvil has previously denied such claims, saying, “I didn’t have any doubts.” “As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented,” Desronvil said in a statement posted by Paltzik last month. On Thursday, Desronvil said he “definitely listened” to the other jurors, but added that “some moments in that deliberation room felt like, that decisions would be swayed towards one way.” McEnany asked Desronvil whether he had reasonable doubt. He replied: “No.” He said he had a lot of evidence to support his reasoning, but declined to share it. He did, however, say he thought Clancy had thought out the murders, stating how “methodical” he believed she had been “in the execution of the children.” “That was really big for me,” he added. “I thought it was logical.” Clancy, who was accused of strangling her three young children to death using exercise bands before allegedly throwing herself out of her home’s second-story window, could have been convicted of first-degree murder, or deemed not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The jury could have also convicted Clancy of lesser charges — second-degree murder or manslaughter. The other 11 jurors were poised to acquit Clancy by the insanity standard, they have said. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings and was therefore unaware of her actions and unable to control herself. The prosecution, however, argued that Clancy was not in psychosis when she killed her children, and that she planned the strangulations ahead of time. The case made global headlines and women showed up in droves to support Clancy at the courthouse and online. For those inside the courtroom, one piece of evidence in particular, from her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, made an impression, Desronvil said: a recording of the 911 call he placed when he found Clancy outside their home, injured after an attempted suicide. “It was surreal,” Desronvil said of hearing that recording. “Hearing the pain in his voice, hearing the desperation from that clip, it was surreal.” Desronvil said he realized his identity was going to be public the day after the mistrial, as the holdout juror was referred to as “he” and “him” multiple times. Desronvil was one of only three male jurors. Since then, he said, media outlets have swarmed his home. Despite this, he acknowledged, if he was called to be a juror again, he would do so. Reddington, when speaking with NBC News last month about the holdout juror, defended Desronvil’s right to his own opinion. “He’s got every right to do that, and I would defend that right, but not to refuse to apply the law,” Reddington said at the time. Desronvil has since tried to shift attention away from himself and back to Clancy’s children, visiting a park dedicated to the slain kids with McEnany. He calls them “the three angels.” “What I would like the world to know about me is that I do extremely care about people, especially children, because children are extremely innocent,” Desronvil said. Desronvil said he had “no idea” how big of a deal this case was in the Boston suburbs and around the country. “Even during jury selection, I had no idea of this case,” he said. Clancy’s future is still unclear. She remains in Tewksbury Hospital while it is determined whether she will be retried. She will be back in court in November for another status hearing to decide the future of the case. articles.body: A passenger flight heading to a popular European destination made a sudden U-turn less than an hour into its journey. British Airways Flight 2660 was traveling from London Gatwick Airport to Faro, Portugal, on Oct. 13 when the aircraft reversed course over France and returned to London, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24. A British Airways spokesperson told Fox News Digital the aircraft needed to divert following a "minor technical issue." articles.title: Exclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war
articles.summary: Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday.
articles.body: Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday. The stark development comes amid an increasingly bitter public feud between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky. In recent days, the White House struck a highly criticized deal to import Russian diesel and heaped increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russia’s oil infrastructure. Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and has since announced Ukraine would continue striking Russian refineries. For months, Zelensky has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of the US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which are one of the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile. But the interceptors are both expensive and in short supply globally, as other countries have burned through their stockpiles or sought to shore up their own defense systems amid the war in Iran. The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.” Russian ballistic missiles hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv during that attack overnight into Wednesday morning. Four people in Kyiv were killed and 25 injured on that day. The Ukrainian Air Force previously said it intercepted four Russian ballistic missiles while defending against that attack, which suggests it used the last few Patriots it had. It’s not thought to be the first time Ukraine has fully run out of Patriot interceptors and Zelensky has been publicly vocal about his constant struggle to obtain more stocks. In mid-August, CNN became the first media outlet to be given access to a Patriot system on Ukrainian territory, and at the time Ukrainian officials revealed the country had pretty much run out of interceptors. Zelensky told CNN in August that his days are spent on “millions” of phone calls with allies, working to make deals for more Patriots. At the time, he said Ukraine only had a tenth of the interceptor missiles it urgently needed. A month later, the Ukrainian president struck a more hopeful tone – claiming that the country “will receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles” from the United States. But US President Donald Trump ultimately declined to say whether he agreed to that, and a license never materialized. Tensions between Zelensky and Trump have bubbled over in recent days amid Washington’s request that Kyiv halt its strikes on Russian fuel facilities, even as Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Zelensky told the Financial Times in a fiery interview that he could only agree to halt energy strikes on Russia if he was given more Patriot interceptors at a “minimum.” He added that “when he asked for more air defenses the American response was to weaken Starlink’s service.” In a public statement on Wednesday, he pleaded once again for more stocks, saying: “The American president has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor. We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.” Ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump has increasingly blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, despite the Iran war playing a more significant role in the fuel price spikes. Earlier this week, the Trump administration warned Ukraine and allies in Europe that the US could suspend European purchases of US weapons and intelligence sharing for Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy facilities, two European officials told CNN. The warnings from the State Department and the Pentagon were sent over the weekend to officials in Ukraine and Europe, including communications from the US military directly to Ukrainian commanders. Trump has since insisted that the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. If the administration did decide to suspend European weapons purchases — which take place via a mechanism called the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL — that would threaten any future shipments of the Patriot interceptors used to defend against ballistic missiles. Ukraine says Starshield not fully restored Running out of Patriot interceptors is far from the only problem plaguing Ukraine this week, as the country also contends with disruptions to intelligence sharing and restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, called Starshield. Ukrainian authorities said they were caught off-guard this week by a throttling of Starshield, which disrupted military operations, logistics and the interception of jet-powered drone attacks. By Thursday, Starshield operations were partially restored, but Ukrainian officials indicated there are still some issues for high-speed military ordnance. SpaceX CEO Musk said on his social media platform X that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, also noting that any limits on its speed or usage are up to the US military and president. CNN has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. A Ukrainian Defense Ministry Source told CNN on Thursday that “as of now, Starshield’s operations have resumed and are continuing.” The source added that the ministry is talking with all parties involved “to determine all the causes and circumstances of yesterday’s restrictions.” Meanwhile, Zelensky indicated that some restrictions are still in place. The Ukrainian president said on Thursday morning that Russia had launched more than 850 attack drones since midnight “at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.” Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, Denys Sienik, echoed that Starshield speeds have improved but are not fully restored. “We hope all will be resumed to the previous level,” he told CNN. Kyiv has received no response from SpaceX or the Pentagon, another Ukrainian official told CNN. A Ukrainian drone commander who spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity said that his unit experienced restrictions on Starlink operations on Wednesday, which prevented some strike drones from reaching their targets. The commander said his unit did not launch any strikes on Thursday due to adverse weather, but other units were operating normally.

articles.title: Trump says Fort Hood US shooter execution will not be livestreamed
articles.summary: US president reverses Pentagon’s plan to publicly stream execution of Nidal Malik Hasan after outcry.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said that the execution of a man who killed several military personnel at the Fort Hood military base in 2009 will not be livestreamed.

The statement on Thursday represented a reversal for the administration, with the Pentagon saying last week the execution would be livestreamed and Trump saying he “absolutely” supported the plan. The public killing would have been the first of its kind in the US since 1936, with successive administrations criticising foreign governments for conducting such executions.

In his post, Trump called the convicted gunman, Nidal Malik Hasan, a “very bad and evil man”. He also accused the administration of former President Barack Obama of an “intelligence failure” ahead of the attack in Texas, which killed 13.

“With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” the US president wrote.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump said, adding that immediate family members of victims would be able to view the execution.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced last week that the execution would be “public”.

“Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said in an interview with right-wing media figure Jack Posobiec.

He added that the execution would take place on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (18:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.

The announcement was met with condemnation from some lawmakers, including members of Trump’s own Republican Party.

Some experts said livestreaming the killing could violate domestic US law that prevents the transmission of obscene, indecent, or graphic material. Some have argued it would be impossible to ensure minors were not able to access the livestream.

Critics have also questioned Hegseth’s claim that a public execution would serve as a deterrent, instead risking glorifying the attacker and inspiring copycats.

articles.title: US teen held over Hindu temple attack plot: Is anti-Indian racism rising?
articles.summary: Illinois teen who allegedly said he ‘couldn’t wait’ to kill Indians is arrested over a Hindu temple attack plot.
articles.body:
A 19-year-old American who expressed ⁠white supremacist ⁠views has been arrested on the day United States police believe he tried to attack a Hindu place of worship.

Police in the state of Illinois say they have thwarted a potential mass shooting and arrested Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from the Chicago suburb of Palatine.

Prosecutors say he told colleagues he “couldn’t wait” to kill Indian people.

The case comes amid mounting concern among Indian Americans about hostility towards their community, fuelled by bitter political fights over immigration and skilled-worker visas.

So what do we know about the alleged plot, and is anti-Indian racism really on the rise in the US?

Investigators say they believe Paporakis planned to attack the largest Hindu temple in Aurora, about 40 miles (65km) southwest of the Chicago suburb of Palatine in Illinois.

“However, the specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation,” police said.

Paporakis allegedly told colleagues that Sunday would be “a special day”.

According to prosecutors, a work colleague told investigators that Paporakis telephoned him on Sunday afternoon, saying his gun had jammed, ABC7 Chicago reported. He allegedly told his coworker he had left “super fast” without being seen.

He allegedly sent a video of the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to try again once it was repaired, Fox 32 Chicago reported.

Two co-workers called police. Officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect then arrested him as he left his home.

“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” said Palatine Police Chief William Nord.

Paporakis faces felony charges of “making a terrorist threat” and “unlawful possession of a weapon”.

On Wednesday, a judge ordered him to be held in jail before a trial.

Prosecutors say Paporakis openly described himself to colleagues at work as a white supremacist.

He allegedly sent a co-worker an eight-page document titled, Why I fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto), according to a court document obtained by The Associated Press news agency.

It described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and set out a plan to kill as many of them as possible.

In it, he allegedly referred to himself as “a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”.

According to prosecutors, he wrote that he had been planning the attack for two years and had researched his target using YouTube and Google Street View, Fox 32 reported.

Prosecutors also said he had mental health issues and lived with his mother, according to ABC7.

A search of his home turned up an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, a gas canister labelled with a slur aimed at South Asians and items bearing Nazi symbolism.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) does not count crimes against Indian Americans as a specific category. The closest measures are crimes against Hindus and Sikhs, most of whom in the US trace their roots to India.

Anti-Sikh crimes appear to be climbing. Police reported 234 anti-Sikh offences to the FBI in the 12 months to October, up from 183 in the previous 12 months, a rise of about 28 percent.

Anti-Hindu offences have remained lower and broadly steady, at 63 over the past two years, or two to three a month.

However, Hindu temples have been targeted.

Over two nights in late June 2025, an estimated 20 to 30 rounds were fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside, according to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. No one was hurt.

Two months later, Illinois Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi condemned a break-in and vandalism at a Hindu temple in Santa Clara, California, saying incidents targeting Hindu temples across the US “are on the rise”.

A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) found the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.

Indian Americans say they are feeling it, too. A Carnegie Endowment for International Peace survey of 1,000 Indian Americans, conducted by YouGov between November 2025 and January 2026, found that one in four had been verbally abused with slurs since the start of 2025.

Nine percent said they had been physically threatened, and 4 percent physically assaulted.

Almost one in five said they had avoided wearing Indian dress in public.

Yet the survey also found no significant change in the number of people reporting personal discrimination since 2020.

Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asian studies at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies and a co-author of the Carnegie survey, said the threat is growing.

“White supremacist extremism is clearly rising,” he told Al Jazeera. “Hostility towards Indians has particularly increased among the MAGA right in President Trump’s second term.”

Much of the hostility has been driven by fights over immigration, researchers say. Trump campaigned on the issue of immigration in the lead-up to the presidential election of 2024, and has launched sweeping restrictions on immigration – including “military-style” federal raids on immigrant communities, resulting in the deaths of some activists – since returning to the White House in January 2025.

Indians receive more than 70 percent of H-1B visas, which US employers use to bring skilled foreign workers to the country. Spikes in online hate have followed political rows over the programme.

In July 2025, President Donald Trump criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India. Days later, amid a trade dispute, he wrote on Truth Social that India and Russia could “take their dead economies down together”. That September, he imposed a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions. US courts are still deciding on the legality of the fee and have currently blocked the payment requirement.

Two-thirds of Indian Americans opposed the fee, the Carnegie survey found.

Figures close to Trump have also displayed anti-Indian attitudes. In September 2024, far-right activist Laura Loomer, at one time a close Trump ally, wrote that the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the presidency. The White House, then under President Joe Biden, called the remark “repugnant”.

Kapur said Vice President JD Vance, whose wife is the daughter of Indian immigrants, had himself used “dog whistle” language, calling H-1B visa holders, most of them Indians, “indentured servants”. “It is therefore not surprising that such incendiary talk can spill over into violence,” Kapur said.

Government accounts have joined in, too. Last month, a since-deleted Department of Homeland Security post featured a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and told him to “get off our roads”. The post came amid a Trump administration campaign to highlight the presence of undocumented immigrants in commercial trucking, particularly Sikhs and Indians.

Researchers also point to the growing prominence of South Asians in US politics, from Harris to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and to the “Great Replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims white populations are being deliberately replaced.

Paporakis is next due in court on October 30.

articles.body: In 2011, Michelle Parker, a 33-year-old mother of three, appeared on a reality TV show, The People's Court, along with her ex-partner Dale Smith Jr to settle their argument over the engagement ring. The disputed ring was worth $5,000 and Parker said on the show that Smith got malicious and vindictive. "He said that he wanted his ring, so I took it off, and I threw it at him," Parker said on the show, which was telecast on November 17, 2011 -- the last time Parker was ever seen. The episode was recorded earlier and the day it was shown, Parker came to Smith to drop off her twins. Smith was the last person to see her but it took the police 15 years to arrest him. Parker's body was never found.Parker filed for a domestic violence injunction against Smith in August 2009, alleging that he smashed her truck window during an argument while holding their young daughter.Years of examining and re-examining evidenceThe day after her disappearance, Parker’s car was recovered on the west side of Orlando, with the decal for her tanning business scraped off its window. Her cellphone was recovered from a lake south of Orlando, police said. Smith was considered a prime suspect at the time, but he was not charged until Wednesday. He has previously denied involvement in her disappearance.But advancements in technology helped reveal new information from cars, electronic devices, phones and computers. And Smith gave conflicting statements over the years.“We were able to better interpret that evidence today than what we were able to do back in 2011,” detective Philip McMican said. Digital forensics revealed more detailed location data and communications between devices used then, he said.Parker's mother said it was the happiest day after Smith was arrested, as she had been holding on to hope throughout the years. “I just knew that one day everything dark would come into the light,” she said. “And it’s been hard, let me tell you. articles.body: In his first televised interview since Lindsay Clancy's mistrial last month, lone holdout juror Michael Desronvil told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany that he stands by his decision not to compromise with 11 others who wanted her to be found not criminally responsible for strangling her three young children. He said he hadn't heard of the case before jury selection and didn't realize how big it would become. He revealed his favorite Bible quote, Psalm 1, which may have prepared him for the ordeal, repeatedly urged the public to focus on the kids and not other aspects of the case. "I call them the Three Angels," he said of the victims. LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL HOLDOUT SAYS HE THOUGHT SHE WAS 'METHODICAL' IN THE 'EXECUTION' OF HER CHILDREN Dawson, 3, wanted to be a firefighter, he said. Cora, 5, reminded him of his own daughter, because they shared the favorite color of purple and were the same age. Callan, the youngest, was only 8 months old. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Reddington has asked for Desronvil's phone records between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. on each deliberation day. "So not during deliberation." Holdout juror accuses journalists of going through his mail, peering into windows Desronvil told McEnany the day after the trial ended, he already saw journalists at his home — including some who snooped through his mail. "We have surveillance cameras, and then we have actual footage of them going through our mail, and then going through the back door, the front door, peeking through the windows," he said. "So we have proof of that." LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ASKS FOR ONE THING IN NEW VIDEO AFTER MISTRIAL DRAMA While the ordeal has been scary enough for police to escort his fiancée to and from his home, he said, he has not received "physical threats." "For sure." Desronvil denies lying under oath Before Clancy's mistrial had been declared, Reddington in court accused the holdout juror of lying under oath, a claim Desronvil denied outright. "I answered everything truthfully," he said. Reddington has nevertheless filed a motion seeking an investigation into Desronvil, past domestic violence allegations, probation records and his juror questionnaire, while publicly trying to rebrand the holdout as "the obstructionist." "There was no physical abuse, emotional abuse, financial abuse of any sorts," he said. Charges were later dropped. Despite his experience, he says he'd serve on a jury again if he had to When asked if he would want to serve on a jury again after his ordeal as the only one among 12 who voted to convict, he said it would be tough but that he'd do it for a higher purpose. GOT A TIP? "With the kind of scrutiny that happened to me, it's tough ... to serve on a jury pool again, but I do serve a higher power so I can't be a coward," he said. "If I have to, I will." However, he said, the prosecution's case convinced him that Clancy had methodically and logically planned the "execution" of her children, rejecting defense arguments that she was not criminally responsible due to postpartum psychosis. "That was really big for me, you know, from watching the video and also listening in the courtroom," he said. "The thought process that goes behind … to fulfill the commitment of doing that." articles.title: Iran-aligned Houthis strike Yemeni presidential palace in escalating campaign against Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Several Houthi missiles struck the presidential Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, killing two members of Prime Minister Shaya Al-Zindani’s security detail, Yemen’s internationally recognized government said Thursday.
articles.body: Several Houthi missiles struck the presidential Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, killing two members of Prime Minister Shaya Al-Zindani’s security detail, Yemen’s internationally recognized government said Thursday. The Iran-backed rebels claimed they were targeting an alleged Saudi military operations center inside the compound. In a statement posted by the government’s Ministry of Information, officials said the prime minister was safe following the strike. “Prime Minister Dr. Shaya Al-Zandani and members of the government are safe following a missile attack by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia on Al-Maashiq Palace in the interim capital, Aden,” the statement said. Aden serves as the de facto capital and seat of the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which is backed by the Saudi-led military coalition. The Houthis claimed the strike was part of a declared strategy of targeting Saudi military deployments wherever they are located. “The shelling of the Saudi enemy’s war operations headquarters in Aden comes within the framework of the declared equation of targeting Saudi military build-ups wherever they may be, and considering any military presence of the Saudi enemy a legitimate target for our forces,” the statement said. The Yemeni government did not immediately provide additional details about the type of missiles used or the extent of the damage at the palace complex. The attack came less than an hour after Houthi forces renewed warnings that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe and that they retained the capability to “respond in kind” to ongoing Saudi attacks on Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that recent Houthi attacks, including strikes targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, demonstrate the growing threat posed by the Iran-backed group to Saudi Arabia, regional security and international shipping routes. The coalition also said military operations would continue with the stated aim of degrading Houthi military capabilities and removing sources of support for the group’s war effort in accordance with international humanitarian law. The strike on the palace came amid continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Earlier Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a drone over Khamis Mushait in the southwest of the kingdom, a cruise missile over the western Medina region and another drone in the Eastern Province. The ongoing attacks have raised concerns about energy supplies, commercial shipping and fuel prices, with the Houthis increasingly targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and maritime traffic. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump accused the Houthis of trying to drive up oil prices and suggested Iran was encouraging the group’s latest attacks. “The Houthis are behaving very badly,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “They’ve been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran…hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. elections.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday said the livestreamed execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army major who killed 13 people in the 2009 attack on Fort Hood, would not go forward.

Trump cited the substantial criticism that had accompanied Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan, saying that while Hasan deserved to be executed, it would not be public.

The president, in a separate post Thursday, also dismissed any notion that the job of his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was in jeopardy after a report indicating as much.

Another White House staffer who’s in the spotlight is press secretary Katie Zacaria, who in her first week is finding herself explaining her legal background. Read more here.

Ukraine attacked a Russian refinery early Thursday with its drones, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said “Russia continues its bloody terror” in a post online. The attacks came a day after Ukraine raised alarm after losing access to Starlink services that power its drones. Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii Beskrestnov described the situation as a speed limit placed by SpaceX on Starlink terminals.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Wednesday night said the Starshield loss may have been caused by a “snafu” within the systems operated by the Pentagon. He said he’d ask for a probe into it.

Trump late Wednesday rallied voters in Montana, following a separate campaign stop in Arizona.

On Thursday, the president takes a day at the White House in between campaign trips. He’ll join two telerallies later in the day, one for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who is running for a full term.

Vice President Vance on Thursday travels to Monroe, Mich., for a rally. He’ll also tape a town hall that will air on CBS News on Saturday.

articles.title: A family bought a New Jersey home in 1929; nearly a century later, raising it became key to preserving it
articles.summary: A New Jersey family home bought in 1929 has survived generations of change, but rising flood risks eventually forced its owner to rethink how it could be
articles.body: A New Jersey family home bought in 1929 has survived generations of change, but rising flood risks eventually forced its owner to rethink how it could be preserved. Located on Cedar Bonnet Island beside Barnegat Bay, the house narrowly escaped damage during Superstorm Sandy in 2012 because it had been temporarily raised for construction work. That unexpected escape prompted Amanda Devecka-Rinear to take a closer look at the building's vulnerability. Rather than risk losing a property filled with family memories, she decided to raise it permanently.Why raising the New Jersey family home became essentialAccording to NPR's report, Devecka-Rinear's great-grandfather bought the house in 1929. It later passed to her grandmother, making the property an important link between generations of the family.The house stood close to the ground, leaving it vulnerable to flooding in the coastal community. For Devecka-Rinear, however, it was not simply a building that could be replaced. Its history and personal significance made preserving it a priority.Superstorm Sandy in 2012 brought that concern into sharp focus. The house escaped flooding because it happened to be lifted on supports while construction work was taking place. The temporary elevation kept it above the water that damaged properties elsewhere.The experience showed Devecka-Rinear what a difference height could make. When she moved into her grandmother's house in 2013, she began considering how to protect it against future storms.How Superstorm Sandy changed the family's plansSandy caused extensive damage along the Jersey Shore, leaving many homeowners facing expensive repairs or the loss of their properties. Devecka-Rinear saw the consequences close to home when her father's neighbouring house was damaged so severely that it had to be demolished and rebuilt, NPR reported.The contrast between the two houses strengthened her resolve to act. She wanted to avoid waiting for another disaster before making the family property safer.Permanently elevating the house offered a way to reduce the risk without abandoning the island. The decision also reflected a wider effort across coastal New Jersey to help homeowners adapt to flooding rather than automatically relocate.The financial challenge of lifting the houseAccording to NPR, raising Devecka-Rinear's home to nearly 13 feet above sea level eventually cost more than $140,000. The work required substantial financial planning, and securing assistance did not mean that the project would be easy to afford.In 2017, Stafford Township received funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to help residents elevate their houses. However, the programme covered only 12 households. Devecka-Rinear had to arrange the money upfront and wait for reimbursement, creating additional pressure.She borrowed from family members to cover expenses and needed somewhere else to stay while the construction was under way.Her experience highlighted a problem with assistance programmes that reimburse homeowners after work has been completed. Even when people qualify for financial support, they may not have enough savings or access to credit to begin expensive projects.Individual homes cannot solve the flooding problemClimate change is adding to the risks facing coastal New Jersey. Rising sea levels, heavier rainfall and powerful storms can increase the likelihood of flooding, while sinking land makes the problem more serious in some locations.Research from Rutgers University cited in the report found that sea levels along the Jersey Shore had risen by about 1.5 feet since the early 1900s, more than twice the global average.New Jersey has pursued several measures to reduce flood damage since Sandy. These include strengthening dunes and buying properties in particularly vulnerable areas. Stafford Township, however, has encouraged residents to elevate their houses because the community's position beside the bay offers limited natural protection.Lifting a house can reduce the likelihood of floodwater entering the building, but it cannot protect everything around it. Roads, electricity supplies, sewers and other essential services can still be damaged. Residents may find themselves unable to reach their homes or live comfortably in them if the surrounding infrastructure fails.The township has therefore considered broader improvements, including raising vulnerable roads and replacing sewer systems. A road elsewhere on the island had already been elevated to help residents travel without driving through floodwater.Preserving a family legacy for the futureFor Devecka-Rinear, the project was about protecting more than the structure itself. NPR reported that her grandmother had specified in her will that the house should belong to her granddaughter permanently, reinforcing the family's wish to keep the property.Devecka-Rinear later became involved with the New Jersey Organizing Project, a nonprofit that advocates for people affected by storms. Her experience helped shape her interest in making disaster recovery and home-protection assistance more accessible.Nearly a century after her great-grandfather bought the property, the house remains part of the family. Raising it has given Devecka-Rinear a practical way to protect that inheritance while continuing to live in a place filled with memories of her grandmother.You use AI every day. articles.title: Venezuela’s Maduro pleads not guilty to US conspiracy to torture charges
articles.summary: Maduro and wife appear in New York City court after new ‘conspiracy to commit torture’ charges.
articles.body:
Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have pleaded not guilty to new charges of ‘conspiracy to commit torture’, which were unsealed last week.

Maduro and Flores appeared in a New York City courtroom on Thursday after being abducted from Caracas in a United States military operation in January.

The pair had previously pleaded not guilty to several other charges, including narco-terrorism, cocaine importation conspiracy and possession of machineguns and destructive devices.

Maduro spoke briefly at his January court appearance, days after the US military abduction.

“I am innocent. I am not guilty. I am a decent man. I am still president of my country,” Maduro said then, adding that he had been “kidnapped”.

US Attorney Jamie McDonald said last week that the couple had for more than two decades “engaged in a conspiracy to commit torture, including the torture of United States citizens, in addition to the narcotics trafficking and weapons offences already charged”.

The new indictment said that Maduro and Flores oversaw a system of torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means to target “individuals viewed as disloyal or a threat to their illegal narcotics activity” as well as a “means of repression against the political opposition”.

It pointed to several instances where Maduro and Flores are alleged to have specifically identified individuals to be targeted, asked for updates on the torture, or suggested techniques.

In one instance in 2014, Maduro urged his enforcers to work harder to extract information from detained military personnel, according to the indictment.

“Squeeze them harder,” he allegedly said. In another, Maduro is accused of suggesting sleep deprivation and pouring water on detainees.

Abuses committed under Maduro’s rule included beatings, electrocutions and threatening family members of detainees, the indictment said. US prosecutors did not accuse Maduro or Flores of directly taking part in the torture.

Maduro became president of Venezuela in 2013, and his re-elections, most recently in 2024, were repeatedly contested by opposition figures and outside monitors.

Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro’s vice president, has led the country since Maduro’s abduction in January.

She had initially decried the US action as “illegal, illegitimate kidnapping”.

However, she has since remained close to the Trump administration, including overseeing efforts to open the country’s state-owned oil industry to foreign companies.
