articles.title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
articles.summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.
articles.body:
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.

The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"

Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.

Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.

Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.

President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.

Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.

But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.

The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".

The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.

In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."

Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.

In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."

Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.

According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.

The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.

Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).

Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.

The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.

On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.

A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.

Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.

"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.

Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire

Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump

The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.

The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".

His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".

"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.

Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.

Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.

President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.

Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".

Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.

Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.

That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

articles.body: US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said on Thursday that negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement were progressing at an “incredible pace”, adding that the “big items are done”.Speaking at an interactive session at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Gor echoed external affairs minister S Jaishankar’s assessment of the negotiations, saying the two sides were “very close to landing it”.Asked about the status of the talks, Gor said he did not want to disclose too many details at this stage, leaving it to the ministers to make announcements. However, he maintained that the major issues had been resolved.“We're actively engaged... within three weeks of arriving here, we announced a trade deal. The European Union trade deal took almost 20 years. So we're at an incredible pace, and I am confident that we will get it done,” Gor said.Gor noted that India and the US had been negotiating for a year and a half, describing the pace of progress as “almost an unheard-of pace”.Notably, the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) was concluded in January after nearly 20 years of negotiations.India has maintained that both sides remain engaged in negotiations to secure a mutually beneficial trade agreement.At an earlier session at the Forum, Jaishankar said the countries were working through their differences and that the negotiations were approaching a “landing point”. He added that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remained unchanged.“We are getting there. I am confident that we will have a trade deal here, as you heard Dr Jaishankar say right on this stage, and we are very close to landing it,” Gor said.Gor on possible sanctions against IndiaGor was also asked about the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 and whether India could receive sanctions relief or exemptions under the legislation.“That is a decision for the president,” Gor said, adding that the legislation grants the US president the authority to make that decision.According to Gor, the US president Donald Trump had not imposed sanctions on any country under the legislation so far. He said the bill had been passed recently and that the President would have to make a determination “within the next 10 days or so”. Gor added that he expected an announcement from the White House soon.On September 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. The legislation authorises him to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, including India and China.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Super El Niño will determine which parts of US get rain and snow this winter
articles.summary: This winter is set to feature numerous strong storms affecting the West Coast and southern half of the country, according to NOAA’s official winter outlook.
articles.body: This winter is set to feature numerous strong storms affecting the West Coast and southern half of the country, according to the official winter outlook released Thursday by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The outlook is dominated by the influence of the near-record strong El Niño event. El Niño, which is characterized by above-average ocean temperatures in the tropical Pacific that lead to a domino effect of shifts in weather patterns around the globe, is likely to peak in intensity in December but make its mark throughout the winter months across the Lower 48 states. Given the influence of El Niño this winter, much of the country is expected to be milder and wetter than average, though not necessarily less snowy than is typical, according to NOAA forecasters. Wintry mix for the southern states Given the near-record intensity of the current El Niño and record-warm ocean temperatures globally, there is the potential for any winter storms to bring unusually heavy rains and mountain snows to the regions that lie in their path. Warmer waters enable greater evaporation, and warmer air can carry more moisture, thereby providing storms with added moisture to work with as they strike land and move across the country. While no two strong El Niño winters are the same, most have temperature and precipitation trends in common. That’s because El Niño typically points the jet stream — the west-to-east flowing, cross-country river of air that steers storms — at the southern tier of the US. The result tends to be more storms and wetter and cooler weather in southern portions of the country, while northern states turn drier and milder than average, according to NOAA. (Yes, snow-loving Northeasterners, that typically means less snow on average during strong El Niño winters, especially in inland areas.) However, NOAA meteorologist Jon Gottschalck said that some of the storms along the southern tier may turn northeast along the East Coast, potentially bringing heavy rain and snow to the big cities of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, depending on the availability of cold air. “These storms could be very strong,” Gottschalck said. In addition to above-average precipitation projected for the West Coast and across the southern states, precipitation along the eastern seaboard is also expected to be above average. Across the Southeast and parts of the southern Plains, where El Nino’s cooler trend and increased precipitation set the table for snow, sleet and freezing rain. Exactly how much frozen precipitation these areas see will depend on how cold it gets, and whether the cold air coincides with storms. Although El Niño is likely to be the dominant player influencing winter weather, it is not the only game in town. Other players, such as the polar vortex, will also influence how much cold air and snow falls, especially along the northern tier of the country. A wet winter likely in California California could be hit hard by this El Niño, as reliable seasonal computer model projections are showing the state could see far above-average precipitation for the winter. Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency in the run-up to the El Niño winter, given the potential for significant inland flooding, high winds, heavy mountain snow and coastal flooding from waves riding on top of unusually high tides during any major storms. History has shown that strong El Niños are no guarantee of an unusually wet California winter, but that they do tilt the odds in favor of such an outcome. And El Niño events can be particularly damaging there. A super El Niño in 1997 to 1998 set seasonal rainfall records across the Golden State and caused widespread flooding and mudslides. “While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter,” Ken Graham, director of the National Weather Service, said in a statement. Half the country warmer than normal El Niño also has an influence on severe thunderstorms, which after peaking in spring, normally pick up steam again near and along the Gulf Coast from late fall to early winter. El Niño puts Florida at a particularly higher risk of them during the winter. The script flips in other parts of the Gulf Coast, which are less active than normal, according to Michael Tippett, a climate scientist at Columbia University. Notably, warmer-than-normal temperatures are possible over more than half of the Lower 48. El Niño can’t be blamed for everything — a world warming due to fossil fuel pollution is always playing a role. Winter is the fastest-warming season for most of the US, according to an analysis from the non-profit research group Climate Central. The areas forecast to be drier than normal aren’t quite perfectly in sync with El Niño, but they are confined to the northern tier, where it is also expected to be milder than average. And unusually warm and dry is not the combination that will produce snow. As with winter temperatures, research shows a warming climate has also impacted snowfall over the decades. Annual snow amounts have dropped in nearly two-thirds of the US since 1970, according to Climate Central. Only time will tell just how wintry this winter will be, but El Niño will almost certainly be a main player alongside our warming climate.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar: What we know about the criminal investigation into the US congresswoman
articles.summary: The nature of the investigation remains unclear but various US media reports suggest it is linked to her US citizenship.
articles.body:
US government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation".

The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.

The search follows multiple comments from federal officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.

Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband.

The Wall Street Journal reported that her cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time.

Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports.

Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.

Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.

Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship.

Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams".

US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.

Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he has "no concerns" about her citizenship.

Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000.

According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18.

If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately.

After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker.

Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications.

According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee".

The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship.

Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991.

"[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator."

The BBC has reached out to Omar for comment.

The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected.

According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration.

Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is taken away. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process.

This appears to be where the groundwork is being laid in the current investigation into Omar.

Trump has repeatedly suggested Omar be deported, calling for her to "go back" to Somalia.

At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."

Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd.

After her home was searched, Omar wrote on X: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "I will not be silenced."

Trump has said the investigation into her has "nothing to do with me".

The timing of the federal probe has defied justice department precedent of not taking action against officials running for office this close to an election.

The raid happened with the November midterm elections only weeks away, drawing condemnation from some of Omar's Democratic colleagues, who said she had been subject to relentless "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations".
